title: The Camino de Santiago
hook: walkers from everywhere follow yellow arrows to Compostela

segments.voice: Yesterday, pilgrimage, and two friends on the road to Emmaus whose hearts burned before they knew why. Your line was the road is the prayer. Did you walk anywhere slowly enough to notice? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

A yellow arrow, painted on the corner of a stone wall in a Spanish village. Another one on a lamppost. Another on a rock beside a dirt track through wheat fields. Follow them long enough and they lead to a cathedral. Along the way, a woman with a backpack and a scallop shell tied to it passes a farmer leaning on a gate. He nods and says two words. Buen camino. Good road. Further on, a teenager with blistered feet hears it from a café owner, then from a pilgrim twice his age who limps past him. The words get said so often they start to feel like a blessing. Today, the road those arrows mark.
screen: `YELLOW ARROWS ON STONE WALLS.` → `A SCALLOP SHELL ON A BACKPACK.` → `TWO WORDS: BUEN CAMINO.`

segments.voice: The Camino de Santiago is the Way of Saint James: a web of pilgrim routes across Spain, Portugal and France that all end at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, in the northwest corner of Spain. First, whose road. Santiago is Spanish for Saint James, the apostle, son of Zebedee and brother of John. The Acts of the Apostles records his death in Jerusalem in a single line, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword." That's Herod. Scripture says no more. Tradition says much more: that James had preached in Spain, that his body was carried there, and that his tomb lies beneath the cathedral. The Church honors the tradition; historians debate it. Both can be said honestly. Second, the signs. The scallop shell became the pilgrim's badge. Walkers carry a credential, a little folded booklet, and get it stamped at churches, hostels and cafés along the way. Arriving with it, a pilgrim can ask the cathedral office for a certificate called the Compostela. Third, the people. Some walk out of devotion, some out of grief, some to keep a vow, some after a hard year, some out of curiosity. The arrows don't ask why. Last, the greeting. Buen camino isn't a prayer. It's a wish shared between strangers going the same way. But it carries something the road to Emmaus showed yesterday: the stranger who falls into step beside you may be going the same way home.
screen: `SANTIAGO IS SAINT JAMES.` · `KILLED WITH THE SWORD, ACTS SAYS.` · `A SHELL, A STAMP, A CERTIFICATE.` · `A WISH BETWEEN STRANGERS.` · then, large: `BUEN CAMINO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk a little farther today. Settle first, and breathe. Think of a walk you already take. To the car, to the mailbox, to the bus, around the block with the dog. Choose the point where you usually turn back, and decide to go one corner past it. Picture that extra stretch now. Who might you pass there? If you pray, you can offer those extra steps for someone carrying a hard road of their own. If you don't, just walk them on purpose. And if you meet anyone on the way, a nod is enough. The bell holds the time.
The Camino de Santiago. The Way of Saint James: pilgrim routes that end at his shrine in Compostela, marked by yellow arrows and scallop shells. Today's word.
Your line: buen camino. Today, walk a little farther than usual, and wish one stranger well on their way, out loud or under your breath. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Pilgrims walk, cycle or ride sections of the Camino to the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, carrying a credential stamped along the way, attending pilgrim Masses and greeting one another with "buen camino."

fork.setup: you've walked into Santiago de Compostela with a full credential of stamps. what can you ask for at the cathedral's pilgrim office?
fork.reveal: the Compostela, a certificate for pilgrims who arrive with their stamped credential.

original.note: Greek: James, the apostle's name as the New Testament writes it. Santiago is how Spanish says Saint James.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long hiking trail in Spain.
what it means: pilgrim routes to the shrine of Saint James at Compostela, walked as prayer and marked by arrows and shells.
what a scholar hears: Acts 12:2 records James's death in Jerusalem; the Spanish tomb rests on tradition, which the Church honors and historians debate.
